titleChinese: 早上洗澡还是晚上洗澡好？
paragraphs: Do you need an energising blast of water in the morning to wake you up for the day? Or do you prefer a relaxing, warm shower in the evening to help you wind down as part of your nighttime routine? Maybe you just shower whenever you feel like it. For something so many of us do, this topic is bound to divide opinion and stir up passion from both sides. But is one really better than the other?

After a long day in the outside world, picking up pollutants and allergens on your skin and in your hair such as dust and pollen, a reasonable instinct would be to wash it all off before getting into bed. That's what the evening shower enthusiasts would say. But, says microbiologist Primrose Freestone, no matter the air temperature, you will continue to sweat during the night. Bacteria on your skin then eat the nutrients in your sweat which is what causes BO. Showering at night also doesn't stop you shedding dead skin cells. All this means you may not wake up feeling as fresh as you had hoped. Showering in the morning, on the other hand, can help to remove dead skin cells, sweat or any bacteria you've picked up from your bed sheets. "As a microbiologist, I am a day shower advocate," she says.

But it's not all about cleanliness. Nancy Rothstein, who calls herself The Sleep Ambassador, is concerned with sleep quality. In her view, showering in the evening is an essential part of the 'preparing for bed' routine. "Call it an opportunity to shower yourself with mindfulness," she says. And research backs this up. A systematic review of research published in Sleep Medicine Reviews in 2019 found nightly warm showering or bathing one to two hours before bedtime can improve sleep.

What it all boils down to is when you would like to feel freshest. If you're someone who can't fully relax in bed until you've showered, you're likely an evening shower person. Whereas, if you can't stand the idea of putting on fresh, clean clothes in the morning when you haven't showered, then a morning rinse is probably more your style. Whenever you choose to shower, Primrose Freestone says it's important to clean your bed sheets regularly to remove all the sweat, bacteria and dead skin cells that build up and can negatively affect the effectiveness of your showers.

title: What can magic teach us about the brain
titleChinese: 魔术向我们揭示了哪些关于大脑的奥秘
paragraphs: You've probably seen the impossible happen, or at least thought you have. When a magician makes a card disappear, or throws a ball into the air, only for it to vanish, it seems that they are using amazing powers. But the magic isn't happening on stage. It's actually all inside your brain.

These illusions work because of essential processes that happen in our brains. Our senses provide an enormous amount of information about our surroundings. Our brains have evolved ways of prioritising what's important. We tend to notice the things that are most significant and remember those which have most meaning for us. What we perceive that we see or remember that we saw is actually a mental image.

These mental processes are exploited by illusionists to trick us into perceiving things in a particular way. In one famous trick, a ball is thrown into the air twice and caught and then vanishes into thin air on the third throw. This third throw is actually just a hand movement. Our brains predict that the ball will leave the magician's hand so we think we see it. The same process makes a dog run for a stick when we pretend to throw it.

During a magic show, we are often manipulated to think that we have a freer choice than we actually do. Magician-turned-psychologist Gustav Kuhn highlights how a performer's gaze can direct our attention towards some things and divert it away from others. Even babies naturally tend to follow where someone is looking. Kuhn has become a researcher using the techniques behind different magic tricks to see what we can learn about how the brain works. He's even teamed up with a toy manufacturer to produce magic sets that explain our mental processes.
Understanding these could be important because while magicians use these deceptions to entertain us, others use similar approaches to mislead us or spread disinformation.

title: Beating brain fog
titleChinese: 战胜脑雾的方法
paragraphs: Do you ever wake up with a fuzzy feeling in your head, you can't concentrate on anything, or find your memory just isn't working as it should? You're not alone. 39% of British people said they suffer brain fog on a regular basis in a FutureYou Cambridge study. But why do we get brain fog, and can we do anything to prevent it?

The technical word for brain fog is cognitive impairment. When you have it, you can't think as clearly as you normally can – just as if your brain was actually full of fog. Dr Brennan, a neuroscientist and author, says "Brain fog is different to these short-term disruptions, because it is persistent, occurs regularly and can interfere with the quality of your life, your relationships, and your work". The reality is that no-one knows exactly what causes it, though theories include chemical or blood flow changes in the brain, and low-level inflammation. What we do know are factors that make it worse.

Fatigue, for example, is a key contributor to brain fog, making it hard to stay focused. This is because sleep deficiency can change activity in some parts of the brain, which means processing and recalling detail becomes harder. Pain and anxiety can also contribute to it – they interfere with cognitive speed because they are distracting. There are also medical conditions that can make it worse, like long Covid or autoimmune conditions like lupus disease.

So, if you're suffering from brain fog, what can you do to fix it? One thing you can do is avoid ultra-processed foods (UPFs). Dr Megan Rossi, the founder of The Gut Health Doctor, told the BBC that "UPFs are often low in essential nutrients like magnesium, omega-3 fatty acids and iron, all of which are crucial for brain function and mental clarity". Therefore, we should pack our diets with nutrient-rich foods like whole grains, vegetables and healthy fats. Blueberries are particularly rich in polyphenols and have been shown to improve cognitive function and memory in clinical trials. Hydration is also very important.
So, if you feel a bit foggy, try to get more sleep and consider making some changes to your diet.

vocabulary.entry: **fuzzy** /ˈfʌzi/ adj. 模糊的，昏沉的

vocabulary.entry: **cognitive impairment** /ˈkɒɡnətɪv ɪmˈpeəmənt/ n. 认知障碍（专业术语，固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Cognitive impairment can affect memory and decision-making.
vocabulary.translation: 认知障碍会影响记忆和决策。

vocabulary.entry: **disruption** /dɪsˈrʌpʃn/ n. 中断，扰乱（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The power outage caused a disruption in communication.
vocabulary.translation: 停电导致了通信中断。

vocabulary.entry: **persistent** /pəˈsɪstənt/ adj. 持续的，持久的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: She has a persistent cough that won't go away.
vocabulary.translation: 她有一个持续不断的咳嗽。

vocabulary.entry: **interfere with** /ˌɪntəˈfɪə wɪð/ phr. v. 干扰，妨碍（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Don't let personal problems interfere with your work.
vocabulary.translation: 不要让个人问题干扰你的工作。

vocabulary.entry: **inflammation** /ˌɪnfləˈmeɪʃn/ n. 炎症（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Chronic inflammation is linked to many diseases.
vocabulary.translation: 慢性炎症与许多疾病有关。

vocabulary.entry: **fatigue** /fəˈtiːɡ/ n. 疲劳，疲倦（书面语）
vocabulary.example: She was suffering from physical and mental fatigue.
vocabulary.translation: 她正遭受身体和精神疲劳的双重折磨。

vocabulary.entry: **contributor** /kənˈtrɪbjətə(r)/ n. 促成因素，贡献者（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Stress is a major contributor to heart disease.
vocabulary.translation: 压力是心脏病的主要诱因之一。

vocabulary.entry: **deficiency** /dɪˈfɪʃnsi/ n. 缺乏，不足（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Iron deficiency can cause anaemia.
vocabulary.translation: 缺铁会导致贫血。

vocabulary.entry: **recall** /rɪˈkɔːl/ v. 回忆，回想（书面语）
vocabulary.example: I can't recall her name at the moment.
vocabulary.translation: 我现在想不起她的名字。

vocabulary.entry: **autoimmune** /ˌɔːtəʊɪˈmjuːn/ adj. 自身免疫的（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
vocabulary.translation: 类风湿性关节炎是一种自身免疫性疾病。

vocabulary.entry: **lupus** /ˈluːpəs/ n. 狼疮（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease.
vocabulary.translation: 狼疮是一种慢性自身免疫性疾病。

vocabulary.entry: **ultra-processed** /ˌʌltrə ˈprəʊsest/ adj. 超加工的（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Ultra-processed foods often contain high levels of sugar and salt.
vocabulary.translation: 超加工食品通常含有高水平的糖和盐。

vocabulary.entry: **essential nutrient** /ɪˌsenʃl ˈnjuːtriənt/ n. 必需营养素（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Vitamins and minerals are essential nutrients.
vocabulary.translation: 维生素和矿物质是必需营养素。

vocabulary.entry: **magnesium** /mæɡˈniːziəm/ n. 镁（专业术语）
vocabulary.example: Nuts and green vegetables are rich in magnesium.
vocabulary.translation: 坚果和绿色蔬菜富含镁。

vocabulary.entry: **omega-3 fatty acid** /əʊˌmeɡə θriː ˈfæti ˌæsɪd/ n. 欧米伽-3脂肪酸（专业术语）
vocabulary.example: Salmon is a good source of omega-3 fatty acids.
vocabulary.translation: 三文鱼是欧米伽-3脂肪酸的良好来源。

vocabulary.entry: **iron** /ˈaɪən/ n. 铁（矿物质）（专业术语）
vocabulary.example: Spinach is rich in iron.
vocabulary.translation: 菠菜富含铁。

vocabulary.entry: **crucial** /ˈkruːʃl/ adj. 至关重要的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Water is crucial for all living things.
vocabulary.translation: 水对所有生物都至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: **mental clarity** /ˈmentl ˈklærəti/ n. 精神清晰度（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Meditation can improve mental clarity.
vocabulary.translation: 冥想可以提高精神清晰度。

vocabulary.entry: **pack** /pæk/ v. 塞满，装满
vocabulary.example: She packed her suitcase with clothes.
vocabulary.translation: 她往行李箱里塞满了衣服。

vocabulary.entry: **nutrient-rich** /ˈnjuːtriənt rɪtʃ/ adj. 营养丰富的
vocabulary.example: Fruit and vegetables are nutrient-rich foods.
vocabulary.translation: 水果和蔬菜是营养丰富的食物。

vocabulary.entry: **whole grain** /ˌhəʊl ˈɡreɪn/ n. 全谷物（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Whole grains are an important source of fibre.
vocabulary.translation: 全谷物是纤维的重要来源。

vocabulary.entry: **blueberry** /ˈbluːbəri/ n. 蓝莓
vocabulary.example: Blueberries are packed with antioxidants.
vocabulary.translation: 蓝莓富含抗氧化剂。

vocabulary.entry: **polyphenol** /ˌpɒliˈfiːnɒl/ n. 多酚（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Polyphenols are found in many fruits and vegetables.
vocabulary.translation: 许多水果和蔬菜中都含有多酚。

vocabulary.entry: **clinical trial** /ˈklɪnɪkl ˈtraɪəl/ n. 临床试验（专业术语，固定表达）
vocabulary.example: The drug is currently being tested in clinical trials.
vocabulary.translation: 这种药物目前正在临床试验中进行测试。

vocabulary.entry: **hydration** /haɪˈdreɪʃn/ n. 补水，水合作用（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Proper hydration is important for athletic performance.
vocabulary.translation: 适当的补水对运动表现很重要。

vocabulary.entry: **foggy** /ˈfɒɡi/ adj. 模糊的，昏沉的
vocabulary.example: I feel a bit foggy this morning.
vocabulary.translation: 今天早上我有点昏昏沉沉的。

sentences.english: Do you ever wake up with a fuzzy feeling in your head, you can't concentrate on anything, or find your memory just isn't working as it should?
sentences.chinese: 你是否曾在醒来时感到头脑昏沉，无法集中注意力，或者发现记忆力不如往常？

sentences.english: You're not alone.
sentences.chinese: 你并不孤单。

sentences.english: 39% of British people said they suffer brain fog on a regular basis in a FutureYou Cambridge study.
sentences.chinese: FutureYou剑桥研究显示，39%的英国人表示他们经常遭受脑雾的困扰。

sentences.english: But why do we get brain fog, and can we do anything to prevent it?
sentences.chinese: 但我们为什么会出现脑雾，我们能做些什么来预防它呢？

sentences.english: The technical word for brain fog is cognitive impairment.
sentences.chinese: 脑雾的专业术语是认知障碍。

sentences.english: When you have it, you can't think as clearly as you normally can – just as if your brain was actually full of fog.
sentences.chinese: 当你有脑雾时，你无法像往常那样清晰地思考——就好像你的大脑真的充满了雾。

sentences.english: Dr Brennan, a neuroscientist and author, says "Brain fog is different to these short-term disruptions, because it is persistent, occurs regularly and can interfere with the quality of your life, your relationships, and your work".
sentences.chinese: 神经科学家兼作家布伦南博士说："脑雾与这些短期干扰不同，因为它是持续性的，经常发生，并且会干扰你的生活质量、人际关系和工作。"

sentences.english: The reality is that no-one knows exactly what causes it, though theories include chemical or blood flow changes in the brain, and low-level inflammation.
sentences.chinese: 事实是，没有人确切知道是什么导致了脑雾，尽管有一些理论涉及大脑中的化学或血流变化，以及低度炎症。

sentences.english: What we do know are factors that make it worse.
sentences.chinese: 我们所知道的是那些会使情况恶化的因素。

sentences.english: Fatigue, for example, is a key contributor to brain fog, making it hard to stay focused.
sentences.chinese: 例如，疲劳是导致脑雾的一个关键因素，使人难以保持专注。

sentences.english: This is because sleep deficiency can change activity in some parts of the brain, which means processing and recalling detail becomes harder.
sentences.chinese: 这是因为睡眠不足可以改变大脑某些部分的活动，这意味着处理和回忆细节变得更加困难。

sentences.english: Pain and anxiety can also contribute to it – they interfere with cognitive speed because they are distracting.
sentences.chinese: 疼痛和焦虑也可能导致脑雾——它们会干扰认知速度，因为它们会分散注意力。

sentences.english: There are also medical conditions that can make it worse, like long Covid or autoimmune conditions like lupus disease.
sentences.chinese: 还有一些医疗状况会使情况恶化，比如长新冠（新冠后遗症）或狼疮等自身免疫性疾病。

sentences.english: So, if you're suffering from brain fog, what can you do to fix it?
sentences.chinese: 那么，如果你正遭受脑雾的困扰，你能做些什么来解决它呢？

sentences.english: One thing you can do is avoid ultra-processed foods (UPFs).
sentences.chinese: 你可以做的一件事是避免超加工食品。

sentences.english: Dr Megan Rossi, the founder of The Gut Health Doctor, told the BBC that "UPFs are often low in essential nutrients like magnesium, omega-3 fatty acids and iron, all of which are crucial for brain function and mental clarity".
sentences.chinese: 肠道健康医生创始人梅根·罗西博士告诉BBC："超加工食品通常缺乏镁、欧米伽-3脂肪酸和铁等必需营养素，而所有这些都对大脑功能和思维清晰至关重要。"

sentences.english: Therefore, we should pack our diets with nutrient-rich foods like whole grains, vegetables and healthy fats.
sentences.chinese: 因此，我们应该在饮食中多摄入营养丰富的食物，如全谷物、蔬菜和健康脂肪。

sentences.english: Blueberries are particularly rich in polyphenols and have been shown to improve cognitive function and memory in clinical trials.
sentences.chinese: 蓝莓尤其富含多酚，在临床试验中已被证明可以改善认知功能和记忆力。

sentences.english: Hydration is also very important.
sentences.chinese: 补水也非常重要。

sentences.english: So, if you feel a bit foggy, try to get more sleep and consider making some changes to your diet.
sentences.chinese: 所以，如果你感觉有点昏沉，试着多睡一会儿，并考虑改变一下你的饮食。

title: Can we create the perfect city soundscape
titleChinese: 我们能规划出完美的城市声景吗
paragraphs: Picture your dream living room. You're sitting on the sofa with the window open. What do you hear? Is it the sound of a flowing river? The murmuring of human chatter as friends enjoy a hot drink at the neighbouring cafe? A soundscape is your aural environment – everything you can hear around you, and researchers say the soundscape where you live can influence your wellbeing.

In times gone by, soundscapes would've consisted of the sounds of nature, such as birdcall and the sound of crashing waves. The reality of human life in the 21st Century means that air travel, construction and traffic noises are now in the mix, and agricultural noise means that not even rural life is safe. Noise pollution can lead to heightened stress levels, impaired cognitive function and higher risk of cardiovascular disease in humans, according to an article published by the UK Parliament called 'The effects of artificial light and noise on human health'. Not only that, it can affect the behaviour and life cycles of species which rely on sound.

So, what can be done? Urban design is one trick. In Barcelona in Spain, urban planners designed 'superblocks', where traffic goes around big groups of buildings and the inner streets are pedestrianised, creating space for people and wildlife that is free from beeping horns and humming motors. In a 2025 article published in BMC Public Health, people in these areas reported an improvement in wellbeing, quality of sleep and reduction in noise.

Other techniques include tree buffers, where trees are planted in urban areas to absorb sound energy. In the Netherlands, they have created earth banks next to Schiphol airport to absorb noise from the runways and protect residents in the surrounding areas. England has a vast network of hedgerows – they'd stretch around the Earth almost ten times if lined up! And it turns out they make excellent sound barriers, particularly if the hedges are large, dense and evergreen.

When we think about improving our environment, it's likely your mind jumps to reducing litter and air pollution. But reducing noise pollution is also important, to create a soundscape that works for everyone – people and wildlife.

vocabulary.entry: **soundscape** /ˈsaʊndskeɪp/ n. 声景，音景（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The soundscape of the forest includes birdsong and rustling leaves.
vocabulary.translation: 森林的声景包括鸟鸣和树叶沙沙声。

vocabulary.entry: **aural** /ˈɔːrəl/ adj. 听觉的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The aural quality of the recording is excellent.
vocabulary.translation: 这段录音的听觉质量极佳。

vocabulary.entry: **wellbeing** /ˈwelbiːɪŋ/ n. 健康，幸福，福祉（书面语）
vocabulary.example: We try to ensure that all our employees have a sense of wellbeing.
vocabulary.translation: 我们努力确保所有员工都有幸福感。

vocabulary.entry: **birdcall** /ˈbɜːdkɔːl/ n. 鸟鸣，鸟叫声
vocabulary.example: I woke up to the sweet birdcall outside my window.
vocabulary.translation: 我在窗外悦耳的鸟鸣声中醒来。

vocabulary.entry: **agricultural** /ˌæɡrɪˈkʌltʃərəl/ adj. 农业的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The country's economy is largely based on agricultural production.
vocabulary.translation: 该国的经济主要基于农业生产。

vocabulary.entry: **heightened** /ˈhaɪtnd/ adj. 增强的，加剧的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The attack caused a state of heightened security.
vocabulary.translation: 这次袭击导致了安全警戒级别的提高。

vocabulary.entry: **impaired** /ɪmˈpeəd/ adj. 受损的，削弱的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The accident left him with impaired vision.
vocabulary.translation: 事故导致他的视力受损。

vocabulary.entry: **cognitive function** /ˈkɒɡnətɪv ˈfʌŋkʃn/ n. 认知功能（专业术语，固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Sleep is essential for maintaining healthy cognitive function.
vocabulary.translation: 睡眠对维持健康的认知功能至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: **cardiovascular** /ˌkɑːdiəʊˈvæskjələ(r)/ adj. 心血管的（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Smoking significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
vocabulary.translation: 吸烟会显著增加患心血管疾病的风险。

vocabulary.entry: **life cycle** /ˈlaɪf saɪkl/ n. 生命周期（专业术语，固定表达）
vocabulary.example: The life cycle of a butterfly includes four stages.
vocabulary.translation: 蝴蝶的生命周期包括四个阶段。

vocabulary.entry: **species** /ˈspiːʃiːz/ n. 物种（单复数同形）
vocabulary.example: There are many species of birds in this forest.
vocabulary.translation: 这片森林里有许多种鸟类。

vocabulary.entry: **superblock** /ˈsuːpəblɒk/ n. 超级街区（城市规划术语）
vocabulary.example: Superblocks are designed to reduce traffic in residential areas.
vocabulary.translation: 超级街区旨在减少住宅区的交通流量。

vocabulary.entry: **pedestrianise** /pəˈdestriənaɪz/ v. 将……改为步行区（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The council plans to pedestrianise the main shopping street.
vocabulary.translation: 市议会计划将主要商业街改为步行区。

vocabulary.entry: **beeping** /ˈbiːpɪŋ/ adj. 发出哔哔声的
vocabulary.example: The beeping sound of the alarm woke me up.
vocabulary.translation: 闹钟的哔哔声把我吵醒了。

vocabulary.entry: **humming** /ˈhʌmɪŋ/ adj. 发出嗡嗡声的
vocabulary.example: The humming noise from the fridge was annoying.
vocabulary.translation: 冰箱发出的嗡嗡声很烦人。

vocabulary.entry: **buffer** /ˈbʌfə(r)/ n. 缓冲物，缓冲区（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The park acts as a green buffer between the city and the highway.
vocabulary.translation: 这个公园是城市和高速公路之间的绿色缓冲带。

vocabulary.entry: **earth bank** /ˈɜːθ bæŋk/ n. 土堤（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: The earth bank protects the village from flooding.
vocabulary.translation: 土堤保护村庄免受洪水侵袭。

vocabulary.entry: **runway** /ˈrʌnweɪ/ n. （机场的）跑道
vocabulary.example: The plane taxied along the runway before takeoff.
vocabulary.translation: 飞机起飞前在跑道上滑行。

vocabulary.entry: **resident** /ˈrezɪdənt/ n. 居民
vocabulary.example: Local residents are opposed to the new development.
vocabulary.translation: 当地居民反对新的开发项目。

vocabulary.entry: **hedgerow** /ˈhedʒrəʊ/ n. 树篱（英式英语）
vocabulary.example: The countryside is crisscrossed with hedgerows.
vocabulary.translation: 乡间遍布着纵横交错的树篱。

vocabulary.entry: **stretch** /stretʃ/ v. 延伸，绵延
vocabulary.example: The beach stretches for miles along the coast.
vocabulary.translation: 海滩沿着海岸绵延数英里。

vocabulary.entry: **line up** /ˌlaɪn ˈʌp/ phr. v. 排队，排成行（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: The books were lined up neatly on the shelf.
vocabulary.translation: 书在书架上整齐地排列着。

vocabulary.entry: **sound barrier** /ˈsaʊnd bæriə(r)/ n. 隔音屏障，声障（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: The motorway is lined with sound barriers to protect nearby homes.
vocabulary.translation: 高速公路两旁设有隔音屏障以保护附近的住宅。

vocabulary.entry: **hedge** /hedʒ/ n. 树篱
vocabulary.example: He trimmed the hedge in front of his house.
vocabulary.translation: 他修剪了房子前面的树篱。

vocabulary.entry: **dense** /dens/ adj. 密集的，浓密的
vocabulary.example: The forest was so dense that we could barely see the sky.
vocabulary.translation: 森林如此茂密，我们几乎看不到天空。

vocabulary.entry: **evergreen** /ˈevəɡriːn/ adj. 常青的，常绿的
vocabulary.example: Pine trees are evergreen and stay green all year.
vocabulary.translation: 松树是常青树，全年保持绿色。

vocabulary.entry: **litter** /ˈlɪtə(r)/ n. 垃圾，废弃物（尤指乱扔的）
vocabulary.example: The park was full of litter after the festival.
vocabulary.translation: 节日过后公园里到处都是垃圾。

vocabulary.entry: **air pollution** /ˈeə pəˌluːʃn/ n. 空气污染（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Air pollution is a major problem in many cities.
vocabulary.translation: 空气污染是许多城市的主要问题。

vocabulary.entry: **noise pollution** /ˈnɔɪz pəˌluːʃn/ n. 噪音污染（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Noise pollution can have serious effects on human health.
vocabulary.translation: 噪音污染会对人类健康产生严重影响。

vocabulary.entry: **murmur** /ˈmɜːmə(r)/ n. 低语，喃喃声（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The murmur of conversation filled the room.
vocabulary.translation: 低低的谈话声充满了房间。

vocabulary.entry: **chatter** /ˈtʃætə(r)/ n. 喋喋不休的谈话声（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The chatter of the children echoed in the playground.
vocabulary.translation: 孩子们的叽叽喳喳声在操场上回荡。

vocabulary.entry: **flowing** /ˈfləʊɪŋ/ adj. 流动的，顺畅的
vocabulary.example: The river is flowing gently through the valley.
vocabulary.translation: 河水缓缓地流过山谷。

vocabulary.entry: **crashing** /ˈkræʃɪŋ/ adj. 撞击的，猛烈的（此处形容海浪）
vocabulary.example: We could hear the crashing waves from our hotel room.
vocabulary.translation: 我们从酒店房间里就能听到海浪拍打的声音。

sentences.english: Picture your dream living room.
sentences.chinese: 想象一下你梦想中的客厅。

sentences.english: You're sitting on the sofa with the window open.
sentences.chinese: 你坐在沙发上，窗户开着。

sentences.english: What do you hear?
sentences.chinese: 你听到了什么？

sentences.english: Is it the sound of a flowing river?
sentences.chinese: 是潺潺的流水声？

sentences.english: The murmuring of human chatter as friends enjoy a hot drink at the neighbouring cafe?
sentences.chinese: 还是朋友们在邻近咖啡馆享用热饮时的低声交谈？

sentences.english: A soundscape is your aural environment – everything you can hear around you, and researchers say the soundscape where you live can influence your wellbeing.
sentences.chinese: 声景就是你的听觉环境——你周围能听到的一切，研究人员表示，你所居住环境的声景会影响你的身心健康。

sentences.english: In times gone by, soundscapes would've consisted of the sounds of nature, such as birdcall and the sound of crashing waves.
sentences.chinese: 在过去，声景通常由自然声音组成，比如鸟鸣和海浪拍打的声音。

sentences.english: The reality of human life in the 21st Century means that air travel, construction and traffic noises are now in the mix, and agricultural noise means that not even rural life is safe.
sentences.chinese: 21世纪人类生活的现实意味着，航空旅行、建筑和交通噪音现在也混杂其中，而农业噪音意味着即使是乡村生活也不再安宁。

sentences.english: Noise pollution can lead to heightened stress levels, impaired cognitive function and higher risk of cardiovascular disease in humans, according to an article published by the UK Parliament called 'The effects of artificial light and noise on human health'.
sentences.chinese: 根据英国议会发表的一篇题为《人造光和噪音对人类健康的影响》的文章，噪音污染会导致人类压力水平升高、认知功能受损以及心血管疾病风险增加。

sentences.english: Not only that, it can affect the behaviour and life cycles of species which rely on sound.
sentences.chinese: 不仅如此，它还会影响依赖声音的物种的行为和生命周期。

sentences.english: So, what can be done?
sentences.chinese: 那么，能做些什么呢？

sentences.english: Urban design is one trick.
sentences.chinese: 城市规划是一种方法。

sentences.english: In Barcelona in Spain, urban planners designed 'superblocks', where traffic goes around big groups of buildings and the inner streets are pedestrianised, creating space for people and wildlife that is free from beeping horns and humming motors.
sentences.chinese: 在西班牙巴塞罗那，城市规划者设计了"超级街区"，车流绕开大片的建筑群，内部街道被改为步行区，为人和野生动物创造了远离喇叭声和马达轰鸣声的空间。

sentences.english: In a 2025 article published in BMC Public Health, people in these areas reported an improvement in wellbeing, quality of sleep and reduction in noise.
sentences.chinese: 在2025年发表在《BMC公共卫生》上的一篇文章中，这些地区的居民报告说，他们的健康状况、睡眠质量得到了改善，噪音也有所减少。

sentences.english: Other techniques include tree buffers, where trees are planted in urban areas to absorb sound energy.
sentences.chinese: 其他方法包括树木缓冲带，即在城市地区种植树木以吸收声能。

sentences.english: In the Netherlands, they have created earth banks next to Schiphol airport to absorb noise from the runways and protect residents in the surrounding areas.
sentences.chinese: 在荷兰，他们在史基浦机场旁边建造了土堤，以吸收跑道的噪音并保护周边地区的居民。

sentences.english: England has a vast network of hedgerows – they'd stretch around the Earth almost ten times if lined up!
sentences.chinese: 英格兰拥有庞大的树篱网络——如果把它们排成一排，它们几乎可以绕地球十圈！

sentences.english: And it turns out they make excellent sound barriers, particularly if the hedges are large, dense and evergreen.
sentences.chinese: 事实证明，它们是极好的隔音屏障，尤其是当树篱又大又密且四季常青时。

sentences.english: When we think about improving our environment, it's likely your mind jumps to reducing litter and air pollution.
sentences.chinese: 当我们考虑改善环境时，你的脑海中很可能会想到减少垃圾和空气污染。

sentences.english: But reducing noise pollution is also important, to create a soundscape that works for everyone – people and wildlife.
sentences.chinese: 但减少噪音污染也很重要，这样才能创造一个对所有人（人类和野生动物）都友好的声景。

title: How to deal with milestone birthday blues
titleChinese: 如何应对里程碑式生日的焦虑
paragraphs: When's your next big birthday? How do you feel about that? Do you feel you need to do something spectacular to mark it? Are you excited by the prospect, or dreading the future?

We usually think of birthdays as a time to celebrate, but they can also cause stress and worry. Research suggests that this can be even stronger for '9-enders', the 29, 39 and 49-year-olds who are worried about the milestone they are about to reach. What is it that makes a number that ends in zero so daunting?

New decades can seem like a fresh start where we evaluate how we are doing. The problem is that many of us look for something to compare with. This might be people that we know or that we follow on social media, or just what we think society expects us to have achieved by a certain age. Any differences can lead us to question ourselves. This links to other stresses that can come with getting older.

We might worry that there is limited time to achieve society's expectations. We may also know people from older generations who had health problems at a certain age, and fear that the same thing will affect us.

So, what can we do? Psychologists advise a few steps. Many agree that it's important to celebrate or mark your birthday in your own way. Do something you genuinely enjoy to avoid feeling the pressure of having to celebrate in a particular way. Another key piece of advice that psychologists offer is that we should use the opportunity to reflect on our lives, but in positive ways. First, consider what you have achieved recently and record those achievements. Then decide what you want to achieve next, and what steps you can take to get there. Having achievable goals can help give our lives greater purpose.

If we can celebrate our successes, set ourselves realistic and achievable goals, and find a way to spend our day that we really enjoy, then maybe we'll find it much easier to deal with those big milestone birthdays.

title: Extreme day trips
titleChinese: 当日往返的极限旅行
paragraphs: You can't beat a holiday, but would you ever consider going away for just one day? Extreme day trips are a new trend that squeeze international adventure into just 24 hours. It might sound exhausting, but for lots of people, the appeal lies in time efficiency, budget-friendly prices and the excitement of going somewhere and doing something completely new.

It's possible to zip to cities in your own country to experience new culture, food and geography without ever leaving 'home', though many European extreme day-trippers go abroad. Monica Stott, a travel blogger from the UK, has taken day trips to Reykjavik in Iceland, Milan in Italy and Lisbon in Portugal, all without staying overnight. It all started for her when she flew over to Ireland for work meetings. She told the BBC, "I'd quite often pop over for a one or two-hour meeting and come home. Then I realised I could stay and make a full day of it."
Social media groups advertising extreme day trips are now booming. These groups offer a supportive community for like-minded travellers and are packed with tips and destination ideas.

However, it's not all fun and games. Hours of the day can easily be taken up with long airport transfers, traffic jams, and in many big cities, there isn't enough time to see everything you want to. Critics also point to the environmental cost. Flying significantly contributes to global emissions and makes carbon-neutral air travel aims, such as the UK's Jet Zero, much less likely to succeed. If other forms of transport can be used, such as trains, that can be a better alternative for the environment. Train stations are often located in city centres, so you can be right in the heart of the city in much less time.
So, if you're tempted, pack light, plan smart and consider the best way to travel for the environment and limited time you have.

sentences.chinese: 这听起来可能很累人，但对许多人来说，其吸引力在于时间效率、经济实惠的价格以及去某个地方做全新事情带来的兴奋感。

sentences.english: It's possible to zip to cities in your own country to experience new culture, food and geography without ever leaving 'home', though many European extreme day-trippers go abroad.
sentences.chinese: 尽管许多欧洲的极限一日游者选择出国，但仅仅是在国内旅行也是可能的，快速穿梭于各个城市，体验新的文化、美食和地理，而无需真正离开"家"。

sentences.english: Monica Stott, a travel blogger from the UK, has taken day trips to Reykjavik in Iceland, Milan in Italy and Lisbon in Portugal, all without staying overnight.
sentences.chinese: 来自英国的旅行博主莫妮卡·斯托特曾前往冰岛雷克雅未克、意大利米兰和葡萄牙里斯本进行一日游，全都没有过夜。

sentences.english: It all started for her when she flew over to Ireland for work meetings.
sentences.chinese: 这一切始于她飞往爱尔兰参加工作会议。

sentences.english: She told the BBC, "I'd quite often pop over for a one or two-hour meeting and come home.
sentences.chinese: 她告诉BBC："我经常飞过去开一两个小时的会然后回家。

sentences.english: Then I realised I could stay and make a full day of it."
sentences.chinese: 然后我意识到我可以去那充分利用一整天。"

sentences.english: Social media groups advertising extreme day trips are now booming.
sentences.chinese: 宣传极限一日游的社交媒体群组现在正如火如荼地发展。

sentences.english: These groups offer a supportive community for like-minded travellers and are packed with tips and destination ideas.
sentences.chinese: 这些群组为志同道合的旅行者提供了一个互助的社区，并充满了小贴士和目的地创意。

sentences.english: However, it's not all fun and games.
sentences.chinese: 然而，它并不全是乐趣和消遣。

sentences.english: Hours of the day can easily be taken up with long airport transfers, traffic jams, and in many big cities, there isn't enough time to see everything you want to.
sentences.chinese: 一天中的几个小时很容易被漫长的机场通勤、交通堵塞所占据，而且在许多大城市，没有足够的时间去看所有你想看的东西。

sentences.english: Critics also point to the environmental cost.
sentences.chinese: 批评者还指出了环境成本。

sentences.english: Flying significantly contributes to global emissions and makes carbon-neutral air travel aims, such as the UK's Jet Zero, much less likely to succeed.
sentences.chinese: 飞行极大地增加了全球排放量，并使碳中和航空旅行目标（如英国的"喷气零排放"）更不可能实现。

sentences.english: If other forms of transport can be used, such as trains, that can be a better alternative for the environment.
sentences.chinese: 如果可以乘坐其他交通工具，比如火车，那对环境来说是更好的选择。

sentences.english: Train stations are often located in city centres, so you can be right in the heart of the city in much less time.
sentences.chinese: 火车站通常位于市中心，因此你可以用更少的时间直达城市中心。

sentences.english: So, if you're tempted, pack light, plan smart and consider the best way to travel for the environment and limited time you have.
sentences.chinese: 所以，如果你心动了，轻装上阵，聪明规划，并考虑在你有限的时间里，选择对环境最好的旅行方式。

title: Can books treat mental health conditions
titleChinese: 读书能帮助我们改善心理健康吗
paragraphs: "It opened up something in me that needed to be opened and needed to heal," says Elizabeth Russell, a teacher and librarian from the US state of Connecticut. She was going through a rough patch in life when she found bibliotherapy.

Bibliotherapy is the use of literature to support people with mental health and wellbeing issues. The benefits of non-fiction, self-help books are well documented – results from 'A meta‐analysis of bibliotherapy studies' suggest this type of bibliotherapy can help with conditions such as anxiety and depression – but what about fiction?

'Creative bibliotherapy' may have similar advantages. Ella Berthoud, well-known bibliotherapist and author of The Novel Cure calls it 'the art of prescribing fiction for life's ailments'. But how does it work? If you were to go to Ella for help, she'd start with a consultation. Then, she says, "I will guide you to books that put a finger on feelings you may often have had, but perhaps never clearly understood before."
Proponents of creative bibliotherapy say that immersing oneself in a good book can help readers process emotions, discover coping strategies or even just provide some escapism from life's stresses.

But some experts worry the benefits of creative bibliotherapy are overhyped. Studies suggest reading may improve things such as empathy and self-confidence, but in terms of treating specific mental health conditions, the evidence is weak. Some stories may even cause harm, particularly if they trigger or reinforce the negative feelings someone wants to escape. It seems bibliotherapy is best used in conjunction with other therapies, rather than as a substitute.

In the UK, the Reading Agency's Reading Well programme helps people manage their health and wellbeing with books. The books are recommended by health experts and people with lived experience of the topics covered. But, the organisation's head of health and wellbeing, Gemma Jolly, understands that it's "not a one size fits all." She says, "It's about having an additional tool that might work for some people." Will you give bibliotherapy a go?

title: How to scientifically spot a genuine smile
titleChinese: 如何科学地识别真诚的微笑
paragraphs: They're not the same, are they? The smiles you see when you meet your friends and family compared with what you see from salespeople trying to get you to buy something or management consultants pretending that the bad news they're giving you is actually good news. How can we tell that someone really means it when they're smiling?

There are physical differences between types of smiles. 19th Century French neurologist, Guillaume Duchenne, spotted that there are two sets of muscles that are used for smiling. Unsurprisingly, one set of muscles moves the corners of your mouth. The other tightens the skin around your eyes. He noticed that only genuine smiles triggered the muscles around the eyes, leading a real smile to be named a Duchenne smile. Later research suggests that there are two pathways to triggering these sets of muscles. Those that are around the mouth can be set off voluntarily, while those around the eyes are triggered involuntarily and almost always by our emotions.

A genuine smile has certain physical signs. Typically, if a smile is real, then people's cheeks are pulled up, the skin under their eyes bulges, and crow's feet can be seen at the corners of their eyes. Smiles that aren't genuine often disappear suddenly rather than fading gradually. These fake smiles are not caused by emotions, but they can get mixed with signs of the emotions that someone is genuinely feeling, like a wrinkled forehead caused by worry.

Even ten-month-old-babies have shown that they can identify a real smile. It may be that we have evolved to spot genuine emotion. There's clearly a benefit in being able to identify who to trust, and who may be trying to deceive us. That's not to say that fake smiles are always a problem. They can help to smooth over difficult situations and maintain politeness. But there are times when it's good to know that a smile really means something.

sentences.english: They're not the same, are they?

sentences.english: The smiles you see when you meet your friends and family compared with what you see from salespeople trying to get you to buy something or management consultants pretending that the bad news they're giving you is actually good news.

sentences.english: How can we tell that someone really means it when they're smiling?

sentences.english: There are physical differences between types of smiles.
sentences.chinese: 不同类型的微笑之间存在生理差异。

sentences.english: 19th Century French neurologist, Guillaume Duchenne, spotted that there are two sets of muscles that are used for smiling.
sentences.chinese: 19世纪法国神经学家纪尧姆·杜兴发现，微笑使用两组肌肉。

sentences.english: Unsurprisingly, one set of muscles moves the corners of your mouth.
sentences.chinese: 不出所料，一组肌肉移动嘴角。

sentences.english: The other tightens the skin around your eyes.
sentences.chinese: 另一组则收紧眼周的皮肤。

sentences.english: He noticed that only genuine smiles triggered the muscles around the eyes, leading a real smile to be named a Duchenne smile.
sentences.chinese: 他注意到，只有真诚的微笑才会触发眼周肌肉，因此真诚的微笑被称为"杜兴微笑"。

sentences.english: Later research suggests that there are two pathways to triggering these sets of muscles.
sentences.chinese: 后来的研究表明，触发这些肌肉有两条途径。

sentences.english: Those that are around the mouth can be set off voluntarily, while those around the eyes are triggered involuntarily and almost always by our emotions.
sentences.chinese: 嘴部周围的肌肉可以随意触发，而眼周的肌肉则是不由自主地触发的，几乎总是由我们的情绪引发。

sentences.chinese: 真诚的微笑有一定的生理迹象。

sentences.english: Typically, if a smile is real, then people's cheeks are pulled up, the skin under their eyes bulges, and crow's feet can be seen at the corners of their eyes.
sentences.chinese: 通常，如果微笑是真实的，那么人的脸颊会上提，眼下皮肤会鼓起，眼角可以看到鱼尾纹。

sentences.chinese: 即使是十个月大的婴儿也能辨别出真诚的微笑。

sentences.english: It may be that we have evolved to spot genuine emotion.
sentences.chinese: 有可能我们已经进化出识别真实情感的能力。

sentences.english: There's clearly a benefit in being able to identify who to trust, and who may be trying to deceive us.

title: Can we trust technology in sport
titleChinese: 体育竞赛中应用的科技可靠吗
paragraphs: Use of technology in sports is supposed to be able to provide accurate and instant feedback, with better decision-making and reduced errors compared to human intervention. But is that always the case?

The annual tennis tournament Wimbledon made the decision this year to replace their line judges. These have traditionally been men and women who judge whether the ball is in or out of bounds, but they were switched out for AI that analyses camera footage, which should be faster and more accurate. Despite this, the electronic line calling system failed just a week into the 2025 championship. The ball-tracking technology was turned off by a person accidentally. This meant a point had to be replayed, which resulted in Sonay Kartal controversially winning the game. If technology needs humans to operate it in the first place, whose fault is it in situations like these where things go wrong?

In football, referees often come under fire for their decision-making. But VAR, that's 'video assistant referee', is regularly used in football these days too. A referee can ask for a VAR check, which means that if they are unsure of something, like the awarding of a penalty, they can double-check their own judgement. However, last football season, VAR made oversights which angered a lot of managers, players and fans. They said the system was not fit for purpose and even favoured some teams over others. Despite this, the Premier League's chief football officer, Tony Scholes, said during the middle of last year's season that standards were actually higher than ever. "Before VAR, 82% of the decisions made were deemed to be correct. In the season so far, that figure is 96%," he said.

So, why do we still not trust technology if it often improves a situation? Professor Gina Neff from Cambridge University says that we have a very strong, in-built sense of fairness. "The machine makes decisions based on the set of rules it's been programmed to adjudicate," she said. "Right now, in many areas where AI is touching our lives, we feel like humans understand the context much better than the machine."
Whether you trust it or not, technology is here to stay, including in the world of sport.

title: How can restaurants earn a Michelin star
titleChinese: 餐厅怎样获得米其林星级
paragraphs: What do rubber tyres have to do with delicious food? The answer lies in the story of the Michelin brothers. French inventors Edouard and Andre Michelin created the Michelin tyre company in 1889 and transformed the travel industry. A few decades later, they began publishing a guide to highlight food in restaurants worth travelling for, which, of course, they'd need strong Michelin tyres to reach. Nowadays, the coveted Michelin star – an award given to only the world's finest restaurants – is one of the culinary world's highest accolades. But the rating system is somewhat shrouded in mystery.

The Michelin Guide itself says their inspectors take into account five criteria: the quality of the ingredients, the harmony of flavours, the mastery of techniques, the personality of the chef as expressed through their cuisine and consistency both across the entire menu and over time. But the inspectors are anonymous, and chefs are always kept in the dark about when they are going to visit. "We're never aware of the inspectors' visit," said Julia Sedefdjian, who became France's youngest Michelin-starred chef at the age of 21. "If they introduce themselves, it's only after they've eaten. And often – very often – they never introduce themselves at all."

And how much does the overall ambience of a restaurant play into the ratings? Ideas vary. Chef Maxime Bouttier, who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants across France for 15 years, thinks details like white tablecloths and background piano music can help to tick boxes for inspectors. Despite this, Bouttier's own restaurant doesn't have tablecloths, and his clientele listen to '80s rap while dining, yet his restaurant earnt a star less than a year after opening. The Michelin Guide says a Michelin star is awarded for the food on the plate, nothing else, and that the style and degree of formality have no bearing on the award whatsoever.

Michelin stars can make or break a chef's culinary career. Earning one gives a chef more recognition, more table bookings and can allow them to raise their prices. But there's also the risk of losing one, and with that comes a lot of pressure.

sentences.english: What do rubber tyres have to do with delicious food?
sentences.chinese: 橡胶轮胎与美味食物有什么关系？

sentences.english: The answer lies in the story of the Michelin brothers.
sentences.chinese: 答案在于米其林兄弟的故事。

sentences.english: French inventors Edouard and Andre Michelin created the Michelin tyre company in 1889 and transformed the travel industry.
sentences.chinese: 法国发明家爱德华和安德烈·米其林于1889年创立了米其林轮胎公司，并改变了旅行行业。

sentences.english: A few decades later, they began publishing a guide to highlight food in restaurants worth travelling for, which, of course, they'd need strong Michelin tyres to reach.
sentences.chinese: 几十年后，他们开始出版一本指南，重点介绍值得前往的餐厅中的美食，而到达这些餐厅当然需要他们耐用的米其林轮胎。

sentences.english: Nowadays, the coveted Michelin star – an award given to only the world's finest restaurants – is one of the culinary world's highest accolades.
sentences.chinese: 如今，令人向往的米其林星——一项仅授予世界上最佳餐厅的奖项——是烹饪界最高的荣誉之一。

sentences.english: But the rating system is somewhat shrouded in mystery.
sentences.chinese: 但评级系统有些神秘。

sentences.english: The Michelin Guide itself says their inspectors take into account five criteria: the quality of the ingredients, the harmony of flavours, the mastery of techniques, the personality of the chef as expressed through their cuisine and consistency both across the entire menu and over time.
sentences.chinese: 米其林指南表示，他们的评审员会考虑五个标准：高质量的食材、和谐调和的味道、高超的厨艺技术、厨师通过菜肴表达出的个性，以及菜单中的菜品品质是否长时间内始终如一。

sentences.english: But the inspectors are anonymous, and chefs are always kept in the dark about when they are going to visit.
sentences.chinese: 但评审员是匿名的，厨师们永远不知道他们何时会来。"

sentences.english: "We're never aware of the inspectors' visit," said Julia Sedefdjian, who became France's youngest Michelin-starred chef at the age of 21.
sentences.chinese: 我们从来不知道评审员的来访，"朱莉娅·塞德夫吉安说，她在21岁时成为法国最年轻的米其林星级厨师。"

sentences.english: "If they introduce themselves, it's only after they've eaten.
sentences.chinese: 如果他们自我介绍，那也是在他们吃完之后。

sentences.english: And often – very often – they never introduce themselves at all."
sentences.chinese: 而且绝大多数情况下——他们根本不自我介绍。"

sentences.english: And how much does the overall ambience of a restaurant play into the ratings?
sentences.chinese: 餐厅的整体氛围对评级有多大影响？

sentences.english: Ideas vary.
sentences.chinese: 观点各不相同。

sentences.english: Chef Maxime Bouttier, who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants across France for 15 years, thinks details like white tablecloths and background piano music can help to tick boxes for inspectors.
sentences.chinese: 在法国各地的米其林星级餐厅工作了15年的厨师马克西姆·布蒂埃认为，白色桌布和背景钢琴音乐等细节可以让评审员认可打分。

sentences.english: Despite this, Bouttier's own restaurant doesn't have tablecloths, and his clientele listen to '80s rap while dining, yet his restaurant earnt a star less than a year after opening.
sentences.chinese: 尽管如此，布蒂埃自己的餐厅没有桌布，他的顾客在用餐时听80年代的说唱音乐，但他的餐厅在开业不到一年后就获得了一颗星。

sentences.english: The Michelin Guide says a Michelin star is awarded for the food on the plate, nothing else, and that the style and degree of formality have no bearing on the award whatsoever.
sentences.chinese: 米其林指南表示，米其林星是根据盘子里的食物颁发的，仅此而已，风格和正式程度与奖项无关。

sentences.english: Michelin stars can make or break a chef's culinary career.
sentences.chinese: 米其林星可以成就或毁掉厨师的烹饪事业。

sentences.english: Earning one gives a chef more recognition, more table bookings and can allow them to raise their prices.
sentences.chinese: 获得一颗星能给厨师带来更多的认可、更多的订位，并且提高价格。

sentences.english: But there's also the risk of losing one, and with that comes a lot of pressure.
sentences.chinese: 但也存在失去一颗星的风险，随之而来的是巨大的压力。

title: The dangers of buffets
titleChinese: 自助餐的安全隐患
paragraphs: The dizzying variety of options, the amazing range of flavours, and for some of us, the sheer quantity that you can eat. It's easy to see the appeal of a buffet. It takes the stress out of choosing what to eat - just have it all! But are there risks that we need to think about? Food hygiene specialists suggest there might be.

Restaurant and hotel buffets can be a food poisoning risk. The large number of different dishes and people serving themselves creates opportunities for cross-contamination. Microbes can be transferred from people to dishes, from dishes to people and from one dish to another. Even the air can transfer microbes to your food. It's easy to see how an entire buffet could end up contaminated. Food temperature creates another risk factor. It's easy for food to be kept lukewarm and in the danger zone between 8C and 63C where bacteria and other microbes grow and multiply easily.

Restaurants that manage buffets well can reduce the risks. Hot food should be replaced after two hours and cold food after four. It's important that the old food is disposed of and that containers are not just topped up, allowing the older food to contaminate fresh items. Hot food should be kept above 63C, and cold food should be refrigerated.

However, any attempts by hospitality businesses to reduce risks can easily be undone by careless clients. There are many ways that diners can unwittingly or thoughtlessly increase the risks. Tongs and ladles can be contaminated by those who do not wash their hands, or who reuse their plates when getting a second helping. Food on display can be contaminated by people using the wrong utensil or who accidentally drop the handles into bowls of food. That's before even mentioning those who cough or sneeze near the buffet.

So, to enjoy a buffet, while keeping the risks as low as possible, you should check to see that it is well-managed by the restaurant or hotel, that others are following good hygiene rules and that you do the same. Even so, a buffet is likely to be more risky than other types of restaurants.

vocabulary.entry: **dizzying** /ˈdɪziɪŋ/ adj. 令人眼花缭乱的，使人眩晕的（书面语）

vocabulary.entry: **sheer** /ʃɪə(r)/ adj. 纯粹的，完全的（用于强调）（书面语）

vocabulary.translation: 这座建筑的规模之大令人印象深刻。

vocabulary.entry: **buffet** /ˈbʊfeɪ/ n. 自助餐
vocabulary.example: The hotel serves a breakfast buffet every morning.
vocabulary.translation: 这家酒店每天早上供应自助早餐。

vocabulary.entry: **hygiene** /ˈhaɪdʒiːn/ n. 卫生（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Good hygiene is essential in food preparation.
vocabulary.translation: 良好的卫生在食物准备中至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: **specialist** /ˈspeʃəlɪst/ n. 专家

vocabulary.translation: 她是一位传染病专家。

vocabulary.translation: 在发生几起食物中毒事件后，这家餐厅被关闭了。

vocabulary.entry: **cross-contamination** /ˌkrɒs kənˌtæmɪˈneɪʃn/ n. 交叉污染（专业术语，书面语）

vocabulary.translation: 使用不同的砧板有助于防止交叉污染。

vocabulary.entry: **microbe** /ˈmaɪkrəʊb/ n. 微生物（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Microbes are everywhere, including in our bodies.
vocabulary.translation: 微生物无处不在，包括在我们的身体里。

vocabulary.translation: 这种疾病可以从动物传染给人类。

vocabulary.example: The water supply has been contaminated by toxic chemicals.
vocabulary.translation: 供水系统已被有毒化学物质污染。

vocabulary.entry: **lukewarm** /ˌluːkˈwɔːm/ adj. 微温的，不冷不热的
vocabulary.example: The soup was only lukewarm.
vocabulary.translation: 汤只是微温的。

vocabulary.entry: **danger zone** /ˈdeɪndʒə zəʊn/ n. 危险区域（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Keep food out of the temperature danger zone to prevent bacteria growth.
vocabulary.translation: 让食物远离温度危险区域以防止细菌滋生。

sentences.english: Food temperature creates another risk factor.
sentences.chinese: 食物温度是另一个风险因素。

sentences.english: It's easy for food to be kept lukewarm and in the danger zone between 8C and 63C where bacteria and other microbes grow and multiply easily.
sentences.chinese: 食物很容易被保持在微温状态，处于8°C到63°C之间的危险区域，细菌和其他微生物在此温度下容易生长和繁殖。

sentences.english: Restaurants that manage buffets well can reduce the risks.
sentences.chinese: 管理得当的自助餐厅可以降低风险。

sentences.english: Hot food should be replaced after two hours and cold food after four.
sentences.chinese: 热食应在两小时后更换，冷食应在四小时后更换。

sentences.english: It's important that the old food is disposed of and that containers are not just topped up, allowing the older food to contaminate fresh items.
sentences.chinese: 重要的是，旧食物要被处理掉，容器不能只是加满，以免旧食物污染新鲜食物。

sentences.english: Hot food should be kept above 63C, and cold food should be refrigerated.
sentences.chinese: 热食应保持在63°C以上，冷食应冷藏。

sentences.english: However, any attempts by hospitality businesses to reduce risks can easily be undone by careless clients.
sentences.chinese: 然而，餐饮企业为降低风险所做的任何努力，都可能被粗心的顾客轻易破坏。

sentences.english: There are many ways that diners can unwittingly or thoughtlessly increase the risks.
sentences.chinese: 用餐者有许多方式会在无意或考虑不周的情况下增加风险。

sentences.english: Tongs and ladles can be contaminated by those who do not wash their hands, or who reuse their plates when getting a second helping.
sentences.chinese: 夹子和勺子可能被不洗手的人，或者在第二次取餐时重复使用盘子的人污染。

sentences.english: Food on display can be contaminated by people using the wrong utensil or who accidentally drop the handles into bowls of food.
sentences.chinese: 展示的食物可能被使用错误餐具或不小心将手柄掉入食物碗中的人污染。

sentences.english: That's before even mentioning those who cough or sneeze near the buffet.
sentences.chinese: 这还不包括那些在自助餐附近咳嗽或打喷嚏的人。

sentences.english: So, to enjoy a buffet, while keeping the risks as low as possible, you should check to see that it is well-managed by the restaurant or hotel, that others are following good hygiene rules and that you do the same.
sentences.chinese: 因此，为了享受自助餐，同时尽可能降低风险，你应该检查餐厅或酒店是否管理得当，其他人是否遵守良好的卫生规则，并且你自己也要这样做。

sentences.english: Even so, a buffet is likely to be more risky than other types of restaurants.
sentences.chinese: 即便如此，自助餐还是可能比其他类型的餐厅风险更高。

title: Britain celebrates 200-year anniversary of passenger trains
titleChinese: 英国庆祝第一列旅客列车通车 200 周年
paragraphs: "The railway that got the world on track." On the 27 September 1825, crowds gathered in a small market town in north-east England to witness something that had not been seen before – a train carrying passengers for the first time. It had taken eight hours to travel 48km – around the speed of an average cyclist – but this steam locomotive was a pioneer in the development of modern railways and changed the world forever as rail spread across the globe.

2025 marks 200 years of passenger trains, and the UK is celebrating this milestone with Railway 200 – a year-long programme of events. From guided walking tours along old, abandoned rail routes, to competitions and careers events. Railway 200 organisers have also designed a travelling exhibition on a special train that will criss-cross the UK for 12 months. Admission to the train is free and there are four carriages, each with a different theme. These include a carriage with hands-on, interactive activities which invite people to test their engineering skills. Emma Roberts, Railway 200 organiser, said it is an "unforgettable experience" for visitors.

Also celebrating this bicentennial is Tom Chesshyre, train enthusiast and author of 'Slow Trains Around Britain'. Among what attracts him to train travel is that you can see places off the beaten track out the train window, and you can relax and read a book without worrying about traffic jams. Tom's favourite slow train ride is from Inverness, in the middle of Scotland, to the most northerly station in the whole of the UK in Thurso through "a kind of desolate landscape". Tom says, "You feel like you're taking a train and disappearing from modern life, leaving it behind."

The route Tom crowned 'most picturesque' was a short journey from St Erth in Cornwall to St Ives which travels along a clifftop with the beach down below. Train travel has come a long way since 1825. Today, trains are more efficient and better connected than ever. From the Eurostar, which connects London to mainland Europe through a tunnel under the English Channel, to high-speed routes in Japan and China, the world is on the move.

title: What happens when your job is just too boring
titleChinese: 工作太无聊怎么办
paragraphs: We all know that having too much work and too much stress can lead to burnout, but did you know that the opposite can also be a problem? Have you ever felt that your job was too easy and that everything was just a bit too boring? If so, you might be suffering from rust out.

Rust out happens when there isn't enough challenge to motivate you to keep going in your job. Without some challenge, it can be hard to feel growth in your role. If a job has lots of repetitive and monotonous tasks, it can make it hard to see the purpose of a role. Having a lower level of responsibility at work than before can also make it harder to feel fulfilled in a job. This can affect people who have taken time out from their career for family or personal reasons.

If you think that you might be suffering from rust out, then there are a number of signs to watch out for. You might dread finding your schedule each week and not seeing anything stimulating on it. It might be that you often find yourself clock-watching at work, willing the time to pass. Focus and motivation can drop, leading you to get less done than you had before, or to make more mistakes. You may start to feel apathetic and disengaged towards your job. These feelings can lead to anxiety and depression which can then spread from work into people's personal lives.

Finding yourself suffering from rust out can sometimes be an opportunity. Some experts suggest that self-awareness is key. By taking some time to realise what you are really looking for in work and life, you can take steps to re-discover your motivation. Setting yourself goals and allowing yourself to try new things can help you find a new purpose. Considering what you really need for a job can also lead you to find a new one that's better suited to your goals in life.

vocabulary.entry: **burnout** /ˈbɜːnaʊt/ n. 倦怠，过度劳累（书面语）
vocabulary.example: Long hours and high stress can lead to burnout.
vocabulary.translation: 长时间工作和高压会导致倦怠。

vocabulary.entry: **rust out** /ˈrʌst aʊt/ n. 职业倦怠（因缺乏挑战而失去动力）（专业术语，固定表达）

vocabulary.translation: 当你的工作太轻松、太无聊时，就会发生职业生锈。

vocabulary.entry: **sign** /saɪn/ n. 迹象，征兆

vocabulary.entry: **stimulating** /ˈstɪmjuleɪtɪŋ/ adj. 刺激的，令人兴奋的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The course was intellectually stimulating.
vocabulary.translation: 这门课程在智力上很有启发性。

vocabulary.entry: **clock-watching** /ˈklɒk wɒtʃɪŋ/ n. 盯着时钟盼下班（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Clock-watching is a sign of low job satisfaction.
vocabulary.translation: 盯着时钟盼下班是工作满意度低的一个迹象。

vocabulary.entry: **apathetic** /ˌæpəˈθetɪk/ adj. 冷漠的，无动于衷的（书面语）

vocabulary.entry: **depression** /dɪˈpreʃn/ n. 抑郁症，沮丧

vocabulary.translation: 旅行可以帮助你重新发现自己。

sentences.english: We all know that having too much work and too much stress can lead to burnout, but did you know that the opposite can also be a problem?
sentences.chinese: 我们都知道工作量过大、压力过大会导致精疲力竭，但你知道吗，相反的情况也可能是一个问题？

sentences.english: Have you ever felt that your job was too easy and that everything was just a bit too boring?
sentences.chinese: 你是否曾觉得自己的工作太轻松，一切都有些太无聊？

sentences.english: If so, you might be suffering from rust out.
sentences.chinese: 如果是这样，你可能正在遭受职业倦怠的困扰。

sentences.english: Rust out happens when there isn't enough challenge to motivate you to keep going in your job.
sentences.chinese: 职业倦怠发生在工作中缺乏足够的挑战来激励你持续前进的时候。

sentences.english: Without some challenge, it can be hard to feel growth in your role.
sentences.chinese: 没有一些挑战，就很难感受到自己在岗位上的成长。

sentences.english: If a job has lots of repetitive and monotonous tasks, it can make it hard to see the purpose of a role.
sentences.chinese: 如果一份工作有很多重复且单调的任务，就很难看清一个岗位的意义。

sentences.english: Having a lower level of responsibility at work than before can also make it harder to feel fulfilled in a job.
sentences.chinese: 工作中的责任水平比以前低，也会让人更难在工作中感到有成就感。

sentences.english: This can affect people who have taken time out from their career for family or personal reasons.
sentences.chinese: 这可能会影响到那些因家庭或个人原因而职业中断的人。

sentences.english: If you think that you might be suffering from rust out, then there are a number of signs to watch out for.
sentences.chinese: 如果你认为自己可能正遭受职业倦怠的困扰，那么有一些迹象需要注意。

sentences.english: You might dread finding your schedule each week and not seeing anything stimulating on it.
sentences.chinese: 你可能会害怕看到每周的日程安排，上面没有任何令人兴奋的内容。

sentences.english: It might be that you often find yourself clock-watching at work, willing the time to pass.
sentences.chinese: 你可能经常在工作中盯着时钟盼下班，希望时间快点过去。

sentences.english: Focus and motivation can drop, leading you to get less done than you had before, or to make more mistakes.
sentences.chinese: 注意力和积极性会下降，导致你比以前完成的工作更少，或者犯更多的错误。

sentences.english: You may start to feel apathetic and disengaged towards your job.
sentences.chinese: 你可能会开始对自己的工作感到冷漠和疏离。

sentences.english: These feelings can lead to anxiety and depression which can then spread from work into people's personal lives.
sentences.chinese: 这些感受可能导致焦虑和抑郁，然后从工作蔓延到人们的个人生活中。

sentences.english: Finding yourself suffering from rust out can sometimes be an opportunity.
sentences.chinese: 发现自己正遭受职业倦怠的困扰有时也可能是一个机会。

sentences.english: Some experts suggest that self-awareness is key.
sentences.chinese: 一些专家建议，自我意识是关键。

sentences.english: By taking some time to realise what you are really looking for in work and life, you can take steps to re-discover your motivation.
sentences.chinese: 花些时间意识到自己在工作和生活中真正想要的是什么，你就可以采取措施重新发现自己的动力。

sentences.english: Setting yourself goals and allowing yourself to try new things can help you find a new purpose.
sentences.chinese: 给自己设定目标，允许自己尝试新事物，可以帮助你找到新的意义。

sentences.english: Considering what you really need for a job can also lead you to find a new one that's better suited to your goals in life.
sentences.chinese: 考虑一份工作你真正需要什么，也可以引导你找到一份更适合你人生目标的新工作。

title: How is ginger good for us
titleChinese: 生姜对健康有哪些益处
paragraphs: It's normal for our bodies to not always be in tip-top condition, whether we catch the flu, have aching muscles after lots of exercise or get travel sick. But there's an ingredient that can help with all of that, and it can be used in all sorts of ways.

Ginger isn't just something to have in the kitchen – it's been used as an aid for centuries. Research consistently shows it eases nausea, such as motion sickness, and is recommended as a remedy by the NHS for helping ease pregnancy sickness. Anna Daniels, a dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association, says it's so beneficial because it has "powerful anti-inflammatory properties which assist with reducing inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract and therefore relieve discomfort and settle upset stomachs."

And it can help with more than just nausea. Ginger tea has been shown to help fight colds and flu because it encourages perspiration, which in turn reduces feverish symptoms. Gingerol, a bioactive compound in the spice, has been found to help reduce the risk of infections because it supports immune health, including autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. And if you're sporty, there's good news for you too. Studies by the International Journal of Preventative Medicine and The Journal of Pain found that a daily supplement of ginger eased muscle soreness after intense physical activity.

So, how can you use ginger? It's an incredibly versatile ingredient and can be used in almost anything from tea to biscuits to fiery stir-fries. Many cafes and supermarkets now sell ginger shots promoting health benefits. Emily Jonzen, author of The Goodness of Ginger and Turmeric, suggests grating it, though she advises "it has a strong flavour and a fieriness to it so introduce it to your cooking a little at a time".
So, if you like the taste, you could incorporate it into your diet and see if you feel these health benefits.

title: Life lessons learnt from pocket money
titleChinese: 从零花钱中学到的人生课程
paragraphs: How much pocket money did you get as a child, if any? Was it a regular, weekly allowance, or just occasional one-off payments for chores? Parents around the world have different ideas about the dos and don'ts of pocket money. How much should parents give? Should they track what their children spend money on? And where is the balance between teaching children valuable life lessons and simply spoiling them?

Giving children pocket money offers more than just disposable income – it can provide lessons in financial literacy. One of the first things children can learn is that money is finite – once it is spent, there's no more until the next allowance. This awareness can help children learn how to budget and make good financial decisions. For example, they might spend weeks saving up for something big and exciting, rather than spending small amounts immediately. Making money mistakes while the amounts are relatively small can prepare children for when they start handling larger sums of money as adults.

Some parents link pocket money to household chores, teaching kids that hard work and good behaviour is rewarded. Louise Hill is the CEO of GoHenry – a money management service for children. She says that earning through chores encourages financial independence and "ultimately gives much more satisfaction rather than instant gratification". The downside of this, however, is that kids may only help around the house when they receive payment, rather than seeing it as their shared responsibility. In their adolescence, young people may transition to a more lucrative way of earning pocket money – part-time work such as babysitting.

Pocket money used to mean exactly that – coins or notes that children could keep in their pocket. And when they're young, seeing physical cash is a good way for them to understand money. But in today's digital world, families are increasingly going cashless. Online money management services are emerging in the market, many of them offering a combination of prepaid debit cards and an app that both child and parent can use to track spending. Some even offer gamified money lessons and the option to set up pots to fulfil savings goals. This modern approach is just another way children can be prepared for adult life, where many transactions are digital.

There's no perfect formula when it comes to pocket money, and a lot will depend on family situation and finances. Ultimately, learning to spend wisely, save and even give generously can help children build a healthy relationship with money that can continue into adulthood.

vocabulary.entry: **allowance** /əˈlaʊəns/ n. 零用钱，津贴
vocabulary.example: My parents give me a weekly allowance of £10.
vocabulary.translation: 我父母每周给我10英镑零用钱。

vocabulary.translation: 这份指南列出了使用社交媒体的注意事项。

vocabulary.entry: **spoil** /spɔɪl/ v. 宠坏，溺爱

vocabulary.entry: **disposable income** /dɪˈspəʊzəbl ˈɪnkʌm/ n. 可支配收入（固定表达）

vocabulary.translation: 如今的年轻人比他们的父母有更多的可支配收入。

vocabulary.entry: **financial literacy** /faɪˌnænʃl ˈlɪtərəsi/ n. 金融素养，理财能力（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Schools should teach financial literacy to prepare students for adult life.
vocabulary.translation: 学校应该教授金融素养，为学生成年生活做好准备。

vocabulary.entry: **finite** /ˈfaɪnaɪt/ adj. 有限的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: The Earth's resources are finite.
vocabulary.translation: 地球的资源是有限的。

vocabulary.entry: **awareness** /əˈweənəs/ n. 意识，认识
vocabulary.example: There is a growing awareness of environmental issues.
vocabulary.translation: 人们对环境问题的意识日益增强。

vocabulary.entry: **budget** /ˈbʌdʒɪt/ v. 制定预算，安排开支
vocabulary.example: We need to budget carefully to save for a holiday.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要仔细预算以攒钱度假。

vocabulary.entry: **sum** /sʌm/ n. 金额，款项
vocabulary.example: He inherited a large sum of money from his grandfather.
vocabulary.translation: 他从祖父那里继承了一大笔钱。

sentences.english: How much pocket money did you get as a child, if any?
sentences.chinese: 你小时候有多少零花钱（如果有的话）？

sentences.english: Was it a regular, weekly allowance, or just occasional one-off payments for chores?
sentences.chinese: 是每周固定的零用钱，还是偶尔为家务一次性支付的报酬？

sentences.english: Parents around the world have different ideas about the dos and don'ts of pocket money.
sentences.chinese: 世界各地的父母对于零花钱的宜忌有不同的看法。

sentences.english: How much should parents give?
sentences.chinese: 父母应该给多少？

sentences.english: Should they track what their children spend money on?
sentences.chinese: 他们应该跟踪孩子把钱花在什么地方吗？

sentences.english: And where is the balance between teaching children valuable life lessons and simply spoiling them?
sentences.chinese: 在教育孩子宝贵的人生经验和单纯地宠坏他们之间，如何平衡？

sentences.english: Giving children pocket money offers more than just disposable income – it can provide lessons in financial literacy.
sentences.chinese: 给孩子零花钱不仅仅是提供可支配收入那么简单——它还可以教导金融知识。

sentences.english: One of the first things children can learn is that money is finite – once it is spent, there's no more until the next allowance.
sentences.chinese: 孩子们可以学到的第一件事是，钱是有限的——一旦花掉，下次发零花钱之前就没有了。

sentences.english: This awareness can help children learn how to budget and make good financial decisions.
sentences.chinese: 这种意识可以帮助孩子学会如何预算并做出好的财务决策。

sentences.english: For example, they might spend weeks saving up for something big and exciting, rather than spending small amounts immediately.
sentences.chinese: 例如，他们可能会花数周时间攒钱买一件大而令人兴奋的东西，而不是立即花掉小钱。

sentences.english: Making money mistakes while the amounts are relatively small can prepare children for when they start handling larger sums of money as adults.
sentences.chinese: 在金额相对较小的时候犯财务错误，可以为孩子们将来成年后开始处理更大金额的钱做准备。

sentences.english: Some parents link pocket money to household chores, teaching kids that hard work and good behaviour is rewarded.
sentences.chinese: 一些父母将零花钱与家务劳动联系起来，教导孩子努力工作和良好行为会得到奖励。

sentences.english: Louise Hill is the CEO of GoHenry – a money management service for children.
sentences.chinese: 路易丝·希尔是GoHenry（一个面向儿童的理财服务）的首席执行官。

sentences.english: She says that earning through chores encourages financial independence and "ultimately gives much more satisfaction rather than instant gratification".
sentences.chinese: 她说，通过做家务赚钱可以鼓励财务独立，并且"最终带来更多的满足感，而不是即时满足"。

sentences.english: The downside of this, however, is that kids may only help around the house when they receive payment, rather than seeing it as their shared responsibility.
sentences.chinese: 然而，这样做的缺点是，孩子们可能只有在收到报酬时才会帮忙做家务，而不是将其视为他们的共同责任。

sentences.english: In their adolescence, young people may transition to a more lucrative way of earning pocket money – part-time work such as babysitting.
sentences.chinese: 在青春期，年轻人可能会过渡到更赚钱的零花钱方式——诸如照看小孩之类的兼职工作。

sentences.english: Pocket money used to mean exactly that – coins or notes that children could keep in their pocket.
sentences.chinese: 零花钱过去正是字面意思——孩子们可以放在口袋里的硬币或纸币。

sentences.english: And when they're young, seeing physical cash is a good way for them to understand money.
sentences.chinese: 在他们小时候，看到实体现金是他们理解金钱的好方法。

sentences.english: But in today's digital world, families are increasingly going cashless.
sentences.chinese: 但在当今的数字世界中，家庭越来越多地走向无现金化。

sentences.english: Online money management services are emerging in the market, many of them offering a combination of prepaid debit cards and an app that both child and parent can use to track spending.
sentences.chinese: 在线理财服务正在市场上涌现，其中许多提供预付借记卡和一个孩子和父母都可以用来跟踪支出的应用程序。

sentences.english: Some even offer gamified money lessons and the option to set up pots to fulfil savings goals.
sentences.chinese: 有些甚至提供游戏化的理财课程，还可以选择设立储蓄罐来实现储蓄目标。

sentences.english: This modern approach is just another way children can be prepared for adult life, where many transactions are digital.
sentences.chinese: 这种现代方法只是让孩子们为成年生活做好准备的另一种方式，因为那时许多交易都是数字化的。

sentences.english: There's no perfect formula when it comes to pocket money, and a lot will depend on family situation and finances.
sentences.chinese: 关于零花钱，没有完美的公式，很多事情取决于家庭情况和财务状况。

sentences.english: Ultimately, learning to spend wisely, save and even give generously can help children build a healthy relationship with money that can continue into adulthood.
sentences.chinese: 最终，学会明智地消费、储蓄甚至慷慨地给予，可以帮助孩子们与金钱建立健康的关系，这种关系可以持续到成年。

title: Is your dog reading your mind
titleChinese: 你的狗狗能读懂你的心思吗
paragraphs: Everyone knows that dogs are supposed to be our best friends. Could it be that they know what we are thinking? Whether it's getting excited at the prospect of a walk or knowing that tasty food is coming soon, are our dogs reading our minds?

Now, by mind-reading we're not talking about knowing our deepest thoughts in detail, but various psychologists have suggested that dogs might have a theory of mind. What this means is that they are aware that other creatures, like humans, are able to see and understand things in different ways. In various experiments it appears that dogs are able to identify who is paying them attention. They are more likely to ask for food from someone if there is a reason that the human would know where the dog treats are. If dogs have been forbidden food by someone, they are more likely to try and get it quietly.

As well as these behavioural studies, there are other things that show how dogs are able to relate closely to humans. Brain imaging studies have shown not only that canine brains react to human voices, but that they also show an emotional response to those human sounds which demonstrate strong feelings, such as laughing or crying. Brain scan studies have also shown that human faces also provoke an emotional response in dogs. Other studies have shown that sweat from people feeling scared could make dogs feel more stressed than sweat from happy people.

There is some debate about whether dogs have evolved to respond to human emotions as they have become domesticated or whether this behaviour is a learned reaction to stimuli. Experiments like those described above have also been carried out on wolves that have been raised by humans, who may have learned to respond to their carer's behaviour, but do not have the genes of a domesticated species. Wolves did show some abilities to respond to human emotions, but were less able to pick up more subtle clues.

Whether it's learned or innate, dogs' ability to read human emotions and intentions are one reason that we have included them in our lives for centuries. It's also why they have been successful as assistance dogs, helping their owners to get through everyday life.

title: What are the chances of an asteroid hitting you
titleChinese: 你被一颗小行星撞击的概率有多大
paragraphs: An asteroid ended the age of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Could something as catastrophic as that happen again?

Asteroids are something astronomers closely track. Recently, the asteroid named 2024 YR4 made headlines for its tiny, but real, chance of colliding with Earth in 2032. In February 2025, NASA increased the impact probability of this asteroid hitting us to 2.3%. Scientists have calculated that YR4 is between 40m and 90m in diameter. It would have the power of a nuclear bomb if it was to hit Earth, causing severe damage if the impact was in a populated area. However, Dr Robert Massey of the Royal Astronomical Society urges calm. He said he is not "losing sleep over" the asteroid, but stresses that funding planetary defence and spotting potential threats is essential.

So what are asteroids? They are fragments of rock left over from the creation of the solar system 4.6 billion years ago. They frequently orbit close to Earth pushed by the gravity of other planets, though it was only in the late 1900s that scientists were able to systematically track near-Earth objects and learn this. They found that asteroids of more than 40m across, that's large enough to destroy a city, cross the Earth's path within lunar distance several times a year.

The chance of an asteroid being large enough to penetrate our atmosphere intact and destroy a city is likely to happen once in every hundred years. In 1908, an asteroid exploded over Siberia, injuring people and buildings across more than 500 square kilometres. However, actual impacts aren't as common as near-misses. For example, the asteroid Apophis raised alarms after it was discovered in 2004 because it was estimated to be around the size of a cruise ship. Even scarier, in 1994, the comet named Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashed into Jupiter, and, if it had hit Earth, all life would have been wiped out, just like the dinosaurs were.
So, it's safe to enjoy admiring the night sky because the chances of you being hit by an asteroid are very, very small, even if they're not zero.

title: The way you move may be as unique as your fingerprint
titleChinese: 我们身体移动的方式可能像指纹一样独特
paragraphs: Have you ever been alone in a room, heard someone coming, and been able to identify who it was based solely on the recognisable stomp of their shoes? Maybe you've experienced seeing a group in the distance, too far to recognise faces, but you're absolutely sure one blurry figure is your friend because of the way they're swinging their arms when they walk. Research suggests that a person's movement signature, or the way they move, could be as unique as a fingerprint. So, what makes up a person's movement signature?

We all have a particular way of moving our faces. One person might purse their lips when they're angry. Another might squint their eyes or pull their face into a grimace, and these movement patterns help us recognise familiar people, even in poor visibility. Another reliable clue for identifying people is their gait. The combination of stride length, limb movement, pace and posture form a movement signature that is very difficult to fake. Researchers in a 2005 study called 'Person identification from biological motion' put small lights on key parts of some male walkers' bodies. When the room was dark and their bodies invisible, observers were able to distinguish the walkers using the lights at an impressively high rate.

Movement signatures are deeply human and expressive. "Dance has always been a part of my life." Brenda Loukes is a dancer and artist who uses ink and bleach to portray bodies in motion. "It occurred to me that each body has a unique blueprint for the way it moves". For dance writer Nancy Wozny, dancers who make it onto her list of 'ones to watch' are those who move in a way she's never seen before, like Stephanie Troyak who has a 'sublime awkwardness', reminding Nancy of a foal's 'first steps out of the womb', or how Ching Ching Wong can divide her body between 'wiggly-squiggly' and completely still.
Whether you're dancing professionally or just walking down the street, your movements reveal who you are and tell a story that no one else can replicate.

title: Why some people believe AI is human
titleChinese: 为什么有的人会把人工智能看作人类
paragraphs: After MIT Professor Joseph Weizenbaum created the chatbot Eliza, he became concerned that people who had used the programme started to act as if it was human. This might sound like a modern problem, but Eliza was created in 1966. If a programme from the 1960s was capable of tricking people into thinking it was human, what effect could the large-language-model-based chatbots of the 2020s have?

Modern philosophers and technology experts have discussed whether AI could develop consciousness. Sentience is difficult to define, but the fact that large language models respond by mathematically calculating the probability of certain patterns appearing suggests that it would be hard to consider them to be alive. However, in terms of our responses to them, what matters is not whether they are sentient, but whether they appear to be so.

Large language models are made up of genuine human interactions. While their tendency to hallucinate means that chatbots are not able to provide reliable factual information, they are able to effectively replicate the language used in human communication. Psychologists report that people tend to have a cognitive bias towards forming attachment and trust. Even sceptical technology writers report feeling some emotion towards AI chatbots. Some users have even reported grief when one model has been replaced by a newer one.

This combination of believable human language together with the inability to reliably assess facts can be dangerous. Cases have been reported where people have been encouraged by chatbots to do dangerous or illegal things. The chatbots were able to use language to encourage and persuade, but not identify or evaluate risks. Trust becomes dangerous when it is not accompanied by reason. Also, if people form relationships with AI, then they may spend less time and effort trying to cultivate genuine human relationships. Could the chatbot revolution lead to a world where we struggle to relate to each other?
